title: Questions: indirect, tags and echo
tagline: Asking politely, checking with a tag, and reacting fast — all without sounding rude.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Speaking Parts 3 and 4 — checking and reacting naturally in conversation
why: A direct question can sound blunt when you're asking a stranger for something, and a flat statement can sound unsure of itself without a tag to check it. B2 First speaking examiners listen for natural indirect questions and question tags, and Part 4 sometimes tests the exact word order that both require.

diagrams.title: Making a direct question indirect

after.text: Could you tell me where the nearest pharmacy is?

steps: Start with a polite frame: Could you tell me / Do you know / I wonder.
Keep the question word (where), but switch to statement word order: subject before verb.
Drop the extra auxiliary do/does/did — it isn't needed once the verb is back in statement order.

diagrams.title: The tag always flips the polarity

rows.label: Example
cells: You've finished the essay, haven't you?
You haven't finished the essay, have you?

rows.label: Typical use
cells: checking something you expect to be true
checking something you're honestly unsure about

branches.label: Let's ...
items: Let's ask Miss Vega, shall we?

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: Could you tell me where the museum is?
Do you know if the shop is open?
You haven't met her, have you?
auxiliary + n't + subject + verb — surprise or criticism
repeat the key word, rising intonation, to check or react

examples.text: Could you tell me where the nearest pharmacy is?
Do you know if the museum is open on Mondays?
I wonder what time the bus to Cusco leaves.
examples.note: not even a question mark needed here

use.point: Checking or confirming with a question tag

examples.text: You've already booked the tickets, haven't you?
Nadia isn't coming to training today, is she?
They'll announce the results tomorrow, won't they?

use.point: Special tags: imperatives, let's, and negative words

examples.text: Let's ask Miss Vega for an extension, shall we?
You never check your messages, do you?
examples.note: never already negative, so the tag is positive

use.point: Reacting fast: negative questions, echo questions and short answers

examples.text: Didn't you bring your notes to the revision session?
'I'm thinking of quitting the team.' 'You're thinking of what?'
examples.note: echo question, checking what you heard
short answer, no need to repeat the whole sentence

watch_out.wrong: You like pizza, do you like?
watch_out.why: A tag is only the opposite auxiliary + pronoun, never a repeated full question.

watch_out.wrong: Could you tell me where is the museum?
watch_out.right: Could you tell me where the museum is?
watch_out.why: Indirect questions use statement word order, not question word order.
The irregular tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I', not 'amn't I'.
Imperatives don't have a subject to match, so they always take the fixed tag 'will you?'.
Negative words like nobody/never already make the statement negative, so the tag must be positive.
A quick reacting question repeats only the auxiliary and subject, not the whole sentence again.

dialogue.title: Packing list for the Sacred Valley
dialogue.context: Mateo, Sofia and Liam are checking last-minute details for a school trip, and Miss Vega confirms the plan.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Miss Vega, could you tell me what time the coach leaves on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Seven sharp. You've all got your permission slips signed, haven't you?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Mine's signed. Liam, you haven't forgotten yours, have you?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Of course not. Actually... didn't you say the slips were due last Friday?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Last Friday, yes. But don't worry — bring it Saturday morning, will you?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Will do. Do you know if we're stopping anywhere for breakfast?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Great. Let's double-check the packing list before we leave, shall we?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Good idea. Nobody's bringing snacks for everyone, are they?

items.why: the statement uses 'are' (present continuous), so the tag matches: aren't you

items.sentence: Could you tell me ___ the museum opens?
items.why: an indirect question keeps statement word order — no extra 'does'
'let's' suggestions always take the tag 'shall we?'

items.sentence: Close the door on your way out, ___?
items.why: imperatives take the fixed tag 'will you?'

items.sentence: Nobody warned us about the change, ___?
items.why: nobody already makes the statement negative, so the tag stays positive
an echo question repeats the key words to check or react, keeping normal word order

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with one suitable word.

Let's take the early bus, ___ we?

items.second_end: the opening times of the museum?

items.first: Let's leave a bit earlier than planned.
items.second_start: Let's leave a bit earlier than planned,

items.first: I'm sure you've already met Nadia before.
Nobody informed the team about the schedule change.
items.second_start: Nobody informed the team about the schedule change,

summary: Indirect questions (Could you tell me..., Do you know if...) use statement word order, not question word order.
Question tags flip the polarity of the statement: positive statement → negative tag, negative statement → positive tag.
Imperatives take 'will you?' and 'let's' takes 'shall we?' — they don't follow the usual auxiliary-matching rule.
Negative words like nobody, never or no one already make a statement negative, so their tag stays positive.
Echo questions and short answers let you react fast in conversation without repeating the whole sentence.
